title: Chapter 66 — The Shark Massacre
paragraphs: When, in the Southern Fishery, a captured Sperm Whale is brought alongside late at night after long and weary toil, it is not, as a general rule at least, customary to proceed at once to the business of cutting him in. For that business is an exceedingly laborious one; it is not very soon completed, and it requires all hands to set about it. Therefore the common practice is to take in all sail, lash the helm alee, and then send everyone below to his hammock until daylight — with the provision that until then anchor-watches shall be kept; that is, the crew in rotation, two by two, each pair for an hour, shall come up on deck to see that all goes well.

But sometimes, especially on the Line (the Equator) in the Pacific, this plan will not answer at all, because such incalculable hosts of sharks gather around the moored carcass that if it were left so for, say, six hours at a stretch, little more than the skeleton would be visible by morning. In most other parts of the ocean, however, where these fish are not so abundant, their wondrous voracity can at times be considerably reduced by vigorously stirring them up with sharp whaling-spades — a procedure which, nevertheless, in some instances only seems to tickle them into still greater activity. But it was not so in the present case with the Pequod's sharks; though, to be sure, any man unused to such sights who had looked over her side that night would almost have thought the whole round sea was one huge cheese, and those sharks the maggots in it.

All the same, when Stubb set the anchor-watch after finishing his supper, and Queequeg and a forecastle seaman came on deck to keep it, the sharks were thrown into no small uproar. The two men at once hung the cutting stages over the side and lowered three lanterns, which threw long gleams of light across the murky water; then, darting their long whaling-spades, they kept up a ceaseless murdering of the sharks,* driving the keen steel deep into their skulls, which seemed to be their only vital spot. But in the foaming confusion of that tangled, struggling mass, the marksmen could not always hit their target, and this revealed fresh evidence of the enemy's incredible ferocity. The sharks snapped viciously not only at one another's spilled entrails but, bending round like flexible bows, at their own, until those entrails seemed to be swallowed over and over by the same mouth, only to pass out again the opposite way through the gaping wound. Nor was that all. It was dangerous to meddle with the corpses and ghosts of these creatures. A kind of generic or Pantheistic vitality seemed to linger in their very joints and bones after what might be called their individual life had gone. One of these sharks, killed and hauled on deck for its skin, nearly took poor Queequeg's hand off when he tried to shut the dead lid of its murderous jaw.

*The whaling-spade used for cutting-in is made of the very best steel; it is about the size of a man's spread hand, and in general shape corresponds to the garden tool it is named after, except that its sides are perfectly flat and its upper end considerably narrower than the lower. This weapon is always kept as sharp as possible, and when in use it is honed now and then, just like a razor. A stiff pole, from twenty to thirty feet long, is fitted into its socket as a handle.
"Queequeg no care what god made him shark," said the savage, agonizingly lifting his hand up and down. "Whether Fiji god or Nantucket god — but the god that made shark must be one damn Indian."
